findings.title: Multiple crypto providers no longer fail fast; ties at order 200 are resolved silently by classpath order
findings.body: The old check threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. It is replaced with a sort by order() descending, taking the first, and logging the ignored ones only at debug level. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200. If, for example, both the default and FIPS providers end up on the classpath, the choice is decided only by ServiceLoader/classpath order. The server can then start in non-FIPS mode (or the reverse) without any warning. The ordering is meant to let the lower-order authz-client provider yield to a real one. Ties between real providers should still be an error, or at least be logged at warn. The ignored-providers message is also passed to debugf as the format string and ends with a dangling ", ".

findings.title: New abstract order() breaks every existing CryptoProvider implementation
findings.body: order() is added to the public SPI interface as an abstract method. Any third-party or custom CryptoProvider compiled against the previous interface now fails to compile. A pre-compiled one throws AbstractMethodError, and CryptoIntegration.detectProvider calls order() during sorting, so startup fails. A default method (for example returning a neutral value) would add the ordering feature without breaking the contract.

findings.title: Dead code: two ASN1Encoder results are computed and discarded
findings.body: `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` build encoders whose results are never used. The same values are encoded again in the `writeDerSeq(...)` call below. These look like leftover debugging lines and should be removed.

findings.title: Provider auto-selected by AuthzClient.create throws UnsupportedOperationException for core JCA operations
findings.body: AuthzClient.create() now calls CryptoIntegration.init, which on a standalone client classpath selects this provider. Most of its methods (getSignature, getKeyFactory, getKeyPairGen, getX509CertFactory, getCertStore, getCertPathBuilder, getAesCbcCipher, getAesGcmCipher, getSecretKeyFact, getPemUtils, wrapFactoryForTruststore, ...) just throw UnsupportedOperationException. They could trivially delegate to the plain JDK (for example `Signature.getInstance(JavaAlgorithm.getJavaAlgorithm(alg))`, `KeyFactory.getInstance`). Keycloak core code paths that go through the CryptoProvider, such as signing client-assertion JWTs with an RSA/EC key or loading certificates and PEM keys, will fail at runtime with an unchecked exception. Only the ECDSA conversion helpers and getKeyStore are implemented.

findings.title: Round-trip-only test cannot catch a symmetric encoder/decoder bug and does not use realistic curve sizes
findings.body: The test only asserts that DER → R||S → DER → R||S returns the same R||S. It never checks that the re-encoded DER (`asn1Des`) equals the original JDK signature (`sign`). It never verifies the converted signature against the public key. A symmetric error in the custom ASN1Encoder/ASN1Decoder (for example non-minimal integer encoding or sign handling) would still pass. The key pair is always the default P-256 curve, even for ES384/ES512, so the 48- and 66-byte component paths are not exercised with matching keys. No negative or malformed-input cases are covered either. Adding `assertArrayEquals(sign, asn1Des)` and per-curve key generation would make the test meaningful.
